web_evidence.title: Confessions Of William Styron
web_evidence.note: In a contemporaneous interview, Styron discusses using first person in the novel and explicitly describes switching into an omniscient third-person narrator’s voice for Sophie’s story.

web_evidence.title: Between Tragedy and Wit: Andrew Ewell on William Styron’s Classic, Sophie’s Choice
web_evidence.note: The structural discussion explicitly describes close-third-person accounts of Sophie’s experience woven into Stingo’s first-person narrative.

web_evidence.title: Sophie's Choice: Key Facts
web_evidence.note: Identifies the retrospective narrator as Stingo and the principal point of view as first person, while treating other characters’ accounts as mediated material; it corroborates the first-person frame but does not describe the third-person reconstructions identified by Styron.

person_note: The novel alternates between Stingo’s sustained participating first-person memoir and sustained close/omniscient third-person reconstructions of Sophie’s Polish and Auschwitz past. The quotes independently expose both modes: numerous passages identify Stingo as “I,” while q02450, q02452, and q02460 come from the reconstructed third-person timeline. Styron’s own interview explicitly confirms the switch, and Literary Hub independently describes the same interweaving. Sophie’s first-person confessions, including q02449, are embedded speech and do not create an additional base-person strand. Sources that summarize the novel simply as first person accurately describe its dominant frame but understate the sustained third-person sections; the main residual uncertainty is terminological—whether those mediated reconstructions are subsumed under Stingo’s frame—but the methodology requires ALTERNATING when sustained timelines use different grammatical persons.
